name: ValkeyTimeSeries

status.note: No tagged release yet; you build the module from source, and it is a community project, not an official Valkey module.

summary: A community module, written in Rust, that adds an in-memory time-series data type to Valkey with the `TS.*` commands of RedisTimeSeries plus Prometheus-style label queries, joins and anomaly detection.
intro: ValkeyTimeSeries is loaded into a Valkey server with `--loadmodule`. Each time series is a key holding labels (name-value pairs) and a list of chunks: ordered, non-overlapping blocks of samples, each a 64-bit timestamp and a 64-bit float, stored compressed by default. `TS.ADD` and `TS.MADD` add samples, creating a series if needed; `TS.RANGE` and `TS.MRANGE` read a time range from one series or from every series whose labels match a filter, optionally aggregated into buckets; `TS.CREATERULE` keeps a downsampled series up to date as samples arrive. A retention period drops old samples, actively in the background rather than lazily on query. The command set is meant to be a superset of RedisTimeSeries, so its clients, such as `@valkey/time-series`, the node-valkey client’s copy of node-redis’s RedisTimeSeries package, send the same commands.

Its additions go beyond RedisTimeSeries: compaction rules can chain (minutes to hours to days), filters accept Prometheus series selectors such as `latency{region=~"us-west-*"}`, `TS.JOIN` joins two series on timestamp, including as-of joins within a tolerance, `TS.OUTLIERS` flags anomalies with z-score, IQR, MAD or random cut forest, and metadata commands list label names, values and cardinality. Label lookups use an inverted index: an adaptive radix tree from each label pair to a Roaring bitmap of series IDs. Queries and batched inserts run in parallel across series and chunks, and identical label strings are stored once. It works in standalone or cluster mode, where related series should share a hash tag so a query stays on one node.
strengths: Keeps recent metrics in memory next to the rest of an application’s Valkey data, with no extra database to run
Speaks the RedisTimeSeries API, so existing clients and code can move from Redis to Valkey
Adds Prometheus-style selectors, chained downsampling, joins and anomaly detection on the server
Apache 2.0, written in Rust, with parallel queries and batched inserts across series and chunks
limits: Not yet released: no tagged versions, a small contributor base, and it is not part of the official valkey-io project
Data lives in memory: all retained samples must fit in RAM, so it suits recent, hot data, not years of history
Cross-series queries in cluster mode work well only if related keys share hash tags

worksWith.how: runs as a loadable module inside

goodFor.why: Series are keys of compressed chunks, an inverted label index finds matching series, and batched inserts run in parallel.

specs.data-model: Series keys with labels and compressed chunks of timestamp and float samples
specs.query-language: `TS.*` commands (a RedisTimeSeries superset) with Prometheus-style selectors
specs.secondary-indexes: Inverted label index: an adaptive radix tree to Roaring bitmaps
specs.scaling: Standalone or Valkey cluster; related series share a hash tag
specs.retention: Per series, dropped in the background; chained downsampling rules
specs.deployment: A module loaded into a Valkey server

story: Time series in Redis came from a separate module, RedisTimeSeries, made by Redis Ltd. When Redis moved to source-available licences in March 2024 and the Linux Foundation started Valkey as an open-source fork, Valkey had no time-series data type, and in May 2024 users asked for one; the request is still open. Clayton Collie, an independent developer, started ValkeyTimeSeries in Rust in early 2025 as a drop-in replacement for RedisTimeSeries, and wrote up its design as an RFC in his fork of Valkey’s RFC repository.

Collie presented it at Keyspace 2025, Valkey’s conference in Amsterdam, on 28 August 2025, describing it as faster and more scalable than RedisTimeSeries and adding Prometheus-style queries and joins. Work has continued in the community opensource-for-valkey organisation; by October 2026 the module also offered anomaly detection, label discovery and a differential fuzzer that checks its answers against RedisTimeSeries, but no tagged release.

choices.why: Applications and client libraries already used `TS.*` commands, so a superset of that API lets them switch servers without rewriting code.
Many users store monitoring metrics, and Prometheus’s label-matching syntax and label metadata APIs are what monitoring tools already speak.

choices.choice: A radix tree of bitmaps for labels
choices.why: Queries select series by label; mapping each label pair to a compressed bitmap of series IDs makes intersecting filters cheap even with millions of series.
Valkey modules run inside the server process, so memory safety and lock-free parallel reads matter; Valkey’s own Bloom filter module is also in Rust.

timeline.text: Redis changes licence; Valkey forks it in March, and users ask for a time-series module in May
Repository created in February; presented at Keyspace 2025 in Amsterdam on 28 August
Commits continue through October; still no tagged release
